p.title: Old money: Campaign finance and gerontocracy in the United States

ext.title: Old money: Campaign finance and gerontocracy in the United States
ext.venue: Journal of Public Economics 249 (2025) 105451; online 31 July 2025 (received 8 July 2024; revised 14 July 2025; accepted 15 July 2025)
ext.doi: 10.1016/j.jpubeco.2025.105451 (printed in the PDF). Metadata hint said 10.2139/ssrn.4892936 and PII S0047272725001495; neither appears in the extracted text, so they are unverified. Use the journal DOI.
ext.document_type: Journal article: empirical political economy (descriptive record-linkage analysis, donor-candidate regressions, counterfactual voucher simulation)
ext.coverage: Full extracted text read in four chunks (lines 1-1696, pp. 1-14 including references). Appendix figures and tables (A2-A7, incl. A4-A6 panel results and A6/A7 ideology and wealth figures) are cited but NOT in the extracted text. Data availability: on request. Paul's 63 highlights all fall on pp. 1-13; none carry note text.
ext.research_question: How unequal is money in US politics across generations, and does this inequality affect political representation? (a) Age distribution of donors, voters, candidates and officeholders; (b) whether donors give more often and more per gift to candidates closer to their age; (c) whether seed (early) fundraising depends on candidate age; (d) how a voucher policy would change candidate fundraising by age.
ext.theory: Resource-based account of participation (Brady, Verba and Schlozman 1995) applied to age: generational wealth gaps (life-cycle and cohort effects, Gale et al. 2020) produce contribution gaps, which shape the candidate pipeline through campaign money as a selectorate (early seed money from personal networks; Bonica 2017, 2020) and access (Kalla and Broockman 2016; Austen-Smith 1995). Alternative explanations (public demand/taste-based discrimination, population demographics, electoral institutions; Sec. 1, pp. 2-3) are argued to be less likely drivers. Campaign finance is positioned as one important driver, not the sole one (p. 3).
ext.data: (1) FEC itemized individual contributions from DIME v4.0: over 600 million itemized donations 1979-2020, most 2016-2020; 23 million unique donor IDs; record linkage links 75% of individual contributors who gave in the 2012-2020 cycles, about 17 million donors (Sec. 3.2, p. 5). (2) L2 national voter file snapshot (April 2021): about 208 million registered voters, with date of birth, primary and general turnout history; census age estimates adjust for unregistered and non-citizen populations (Sec. 3.1, p. 4; fn. 8). (3) Candidate birth years for 11,741 congressional candidates 2012-2020 from congressional bios, Project Vote Smart, and L2 linkage; linkage correlation with Vote Smart r = 0.95 (Sec. 3.3, p. 5; fn. 11). Main donor analyses focus on the 2020 cycle because small-donor coverage (ActBlue, WinRed) is near-complete then (Sec. 3, p. 4). Unit and N by table: Table 1 candidate-cycle, N = 6,098 candidates (2012-2020, at least 10 donors per cycle); Tables 2-3 donor-candidate pairs in 2020: Democrats 2,048,581,125 pairs (Donated outcome) and 6,945,203 (asinh amount); Republicans 829,871,280 and 3,964,488; Table 4 non-incumbent House candidates in 2020, N = 931 (challengers and open seats); seed funding uses each candidate first 50 donations. Panel robustness (appendix) about 200 million same-state dyads, 2012-2020.
ext.method: Descriptive: age distributions for 2020 (box plots, medians and dollar-weighted means), generational shares of wealth vs donations (Fig. 6), and birth-cohort representational weight = cohort share of contributions over population share, scaled to 18-year-olds = 1 (Fig. 4). Candidate-level OLS (Eq. 1): average donor age (or dollar-weighted average) on candidate age x incumbency, with cycle and district fixed effects (Table 1). Donor-level linear probability model (Donated x100) and asinh(amount) (Eq. 2): |Age Gap| between donor and candidate, same-state control, donor and candidate two-way fixed effects, separately for Democrats and Republicans, with generation interactions (Tables 2-3; text p. 8-9). Seed-funding OLS with district fixed effects (Table 4). Counterfactual voucher simulation (Sec. 6.1, pp. 12-13): post-stratification reweighting of contributions so that strata (birth year, precinct partisanship in 10 groups, population density in 5 bins) match electoral shares, via inflation factor eta_s = electoral share / contribution share; gamma_c = voucher-program contributions / actual contributions per candidate; log(gamma_c) plotted by candidate age with loess (Fig. 8).
ext.identification: No exogenous policy shock. Within-district variation (Table 1, district FE) and within-donor / within-candidate variation (Eq. 2, two-way FE; donor and candidate fixed effects absorb time-invariant donor and candidate traits, incl. wealth and ideology). Authors state they do not estimate the wealth elasticity or the causal effect of wealth or of policy (pp. 1-2) and call exogenous policy variation future work (Sec. 7). Eq. 2 relies on the age gap varying across donor-candidate pairs within a donor; the text does not test time-varying dyad confounds. Voucher results are a counterfactual reweighting under stated assumptions, not an estimate.
ext.scope: US federal elections (House and Senate candidates and their individual donors), mainly the 2020 cycle; panel robustness 2012-2020 in appendix (same-state dyads only). Population: near-universe of voters (L2), donors (DIME-linked), and candidates. Era: 2012-2020 data, with 2020 as the core cycle. Institution: post-Citizens United, post-McCutcheon US campaign finance (individual limit $2,900 per election cited on p. 11). Not covered: PAC, party and presidential money (excluded in Fig. 5); dark money (explicitly not accounted for, Sec. 6, p. 11).

key_findings.finding: Median dollar of campaign contributions comes from a 66-year-old; mean dollar from a 64-year-old (63.9); median unweighted donor is 59. Only 9% of contribution dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger.
key_findings.numbers: median dollar 66; mean dollar 63.9; median donor 59; 9% of dollars from donors <=40

key_findings.finding: Age gaps in participation: median voter 52, median non-voter 39, median primary voter 59. Average American age 38; voting-age public age 47. Candidates slightly younger than donors; incumbents slightly older. Those gaps are smaller than the gap between donors and general-election voters or non-voters.
key_findings.numbers: voters 52; non-voters 39; primary voters 59; donors 59; US average 38; voting-age public 47

key_findings.finding: Generational shares of donations track wealth shares. Baby Boomers give 53.6% of donation dollars and receive 48.5% of candidate receipts; Millennials give 5% of donation dollars and receive 10.4% of candidate receipts. Millennial candidates get over 66% of their dollars from Silent and Boomer donors plus about 20% from Gen X; Millennial donors supply 4% of Boomer candidates' receipts.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.1 p. 7 (Fig. 6); Sec. 4.1 p. 6 and Appendix A7 for wealth shares
key_findings.numbers: Boomer donors 53.6%; Millennial donors 5%; Millennial candidate receipts 10.4%; Millennial candidates 66%+ from Silent/Boomers; Gen X ~20%; Millennial share of Boomer-candidate money 4%; wealth shares Millennials 4.5%, Boomers 53.1%; contributions Millennials 5.3%, Boomers 52.8%

key_findings.finding: Representational weight rises sharply with age. 35-year-olds are over 25 times better represented than 18-year-olds; the most represented cohorts (ages 70-80) give about 200-300 times more per capita than the youngest cohort.

Average contribution size rises with donor birth cohort. Donors born after 1985 give about $75 on average; donors born 1940-1965 about $200; pre-1935 cohorts about $300. Ever-donors to the $2,900 limit average 63 years old.
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.1 / Fig. 5 p. 6 and Sec. 6 p. 11

key_findings.finding: Candidate age is strongly associated with donor age within districts. Each year of candidate age raises average donor age by about 0.21 years (unweighted) and dollar-weighted donor age by about 0.20 years. Donor-age SD is 5.8 vs 12.5 for candidate age. Incumbents have donors about 8 years older on average (unweighted).
key_findings.numbers: 0.21 (SE 0.01); 0.20 (SE 0.01); N = 6,098 candidate-cycles; incumbent +8.16 years; SD donor age 5.8, candidate age 12.5

key_findings.finding: Within-donor, two-way fixed-effects estimates: donors are less likely to give, and give less, the larger the age gap with a candidate. Paper reports that a 30-year age gap is associated with about a 50% reduction in the likelihood of donating (baseline 0.189 for Democrats, 0.184 for Republicans, x100 scale). Effects are similar across parties on the extensive margin.
key_findings.numbers: Democrats extensive |Age Gap| coef -0.00328 (SE 0.00001); Republicans -0.00317 (SE 0.00003); intensive asinh(amount) Democrats -0.00178 (SE 0.00005), Republicans -0.00218 (SE 0.00008); baseline donating rate 0.189 (D) and 0.184 (R); 30-year gap ~50% lower donation likelihood (authors' calculation)

key_findings.finding: Generation interactions: the age-gap penalty on donating is largest for the oldest and youngest donors (Silent generation -0.00502 for Democrats). For Gen Z, a larger age gap strongly lowers donating but conditional on donating, Gen Z donors give slightly more to more distant-age candidates (Democrats +0.00132; Republicans +0.00335 on the intensive margin, which the text describes as the same pattern).
key_findings.location: Sec. 5.3 p. 9 and fn. 14 p. 9; Tables 2-3
key_findings.numbers: Silent x age gap -0.00502 (D); Gen Z x age gap -0.00332 extensive (D); Gen Z intensive +0.00132 (D), +0.00335 (R)

key_findings.finding: Effect is more pronounced for Democrats, where donor age varies more and ideology is more age-polarized (abstract and Sec. 5.3). Republican coefficients are unexpectedly positive in cycles before 2020, which the authors attribute to lower Republican donor-age variance and missing small donors before WinRed.
key_findings.location: Intro p. 2; Sec. 5.3 p. 9; fn. 3 p. 2; fn. 3 text pp. 2-3
key_findings.numbers: Pre-2020 Republican age-gap coefficients positive; Democratic coefficients similar 2014-2018 and smaller in 2012

key_findings.finding: Seed funding (first 50 donations) is older-donor heavy for older candidates. Within district, a 65-year-old's seed donors are 8.4 years older than a 35-year-old's. Each year of candidate age adds about $6.91 to average seed-donor amount (a 65- vs 35-year-old raises about $207 more per early donor). Older candidates self-fund more, about 6% more per year of age.
key_findings.numbers: seed donor age coef 0.28 (SE 0.02) per year; $6.91 (SE 1.67) per year; ln(self-funding) 0.06 (SE 0.01); N = 931; R2 0.58, 0.46, 0.43; 8.4-year and $207 differences for 35 vs 65

key_findings.finding: Voucher simulation (4 x $25-type credits in Seattle comparison; simulated full participation matching voter turnout): the average candidate under age 30 would raise over three times more funds; candidates over 66 raise less on average, down to about one-third fewer for the average candidate over 80. Threshold age is 66. Intro states the average candidate under 50 would get about twice the share of contributions and candidates below 66 benefit on average.
key_findings.numbers: threshold age 66; under 30 >3x; over 80 about 1/3 fewer; under 50 ~2x share of contributions; example gamma AOC (b. 1989) 2.05; Barbara Lee (b. 1946) and Jamie Raskin (b. 1962) below 0.5

key_findings.finding: Underrepresented young subgroup in the simulation: older Millennials (b. 1985-1989) in Democratic-leaning, high-density districts are 1.45% of the 2020 electorate but only 0.96% of contributions; the simulation raises their share to 1.45%.

Authors reject taste-based age discrimination by voters as the main driver: conjoint studies show public favors younger candidates, over 70% back maximum age limits, and constituent approval is negatively associated with age net of ideology. Party age distributions are close (House Democrats avg 59, Republicans 57). US legislators are the oldest in the OECD, while the correlation between population median age and legislator age across countries is -0.003.
key_findings.location: Sec. 1 pp. 2-3; Fig. 1 p. 2 caption; intro p. 1
key_findings.numbers: correlation -0.003; over 70% support age limits; Congress avg age 58 House, 64 Senate (2022); Democrats 59, Republicans 57

key_findings.finding: Donor-candidate linkage is near-representative: linked and unlinked donors show similar retired/student shares; unlinked donors have slightly more conservative CFscores and larger average donations, which the authors do not treat as material bias.
key_findings.numbers: 75% linked; 17 million linked donors; birth year validation r = 0.95

key_findings.finding: Abstract claims older donors are much more ideologically conservative than younger donors, and that donor-partisanship age gaps exceed those in voting and survey attitudes. The text body does not give the supporting numbers (they are in appendix figures not extracted).
key_findings.location: Highlights p. 1; abstract/intro p. 1-2; Sec. 4 (Appendix A6)

limitations: Paper states it does not directly estimate wealth elasticities or causal effects of wealth or contributions; cited causal evaluation of policy left to future work with exogenous changes (pp. 1-2; Sec. 7).

Small-donor coverage: data before 2020 exclude most small donors (ActBlue and WinRed itemization; Sec. 3 p. 4; fn. 3; Sec. 5.3 p. 9). Pre-2020 Republican coefficients are unexpectedly positive and the party comparison is only clean for 2020.
Dark money (Citizens United-era independent groups) is not accounted for (Sec. 6 p. 11).
Extensive-margin models use donor fixed effects, so non-donors drop out of that estimate (Sec. 5.3 p. 8). Panel robustness (2012-2020) restricted to same-state dyads (about 200 million observations).

Record linkage links 75% of donors; misses occur for different addresses, unregistered donors and name changes. Linkage algorithm designed to limit false positives, which can bias the linked sample (Sec. 3.2 pp. 4-5).

Voucher simulation assumes full participation with donor shares matched to voter turnout, all candidates adopt vouchers and cannot take private money, and simple assumptions about spending and candidate pipelines (intro p. 2; Sec. 6.1 pp. 11-13; fn. 16). Informational costs of vouchers may reduce young participation (Sec. 6 p. 11). Contribution-limit age effects are described as less certain (Sec. 6 p. 11).
Seed-funding model uses only non-incumbent House candidates in 2020 (N = 931) with district fixed effects and no candidate fixed effects (Sec. 5.4 p. 10).

Authors cannot rule out alternative theories of contribution behavior, e.g., political efficacy and inclusion (fn. 2 p. 2). Online small-dollar strategies by younger candidates are an alternative explanation for seed-funding gaps (fn. 15 p. 11).
Cohort vs life-cycle effects are not separately identified in the main analysis; text says generational patterns are interpreted with both (Sec. 1, Sec. 7).
Data available only on request (Data availability statement). Appendix figures and tables (A2-A7) not in the extracted text, so appendix-only claims were not verified.
Reference-list mismatch: text cites (Li, 2022) for online scams, but the reference list has Zhao, L., 2022 (Lemons in the political marketplace). Treat that citation as unverified.

rel.summary_md:
Bonica and Grumbach link DIME itemized FEC contributions to the L2 voter file and to candidate birth years. They show that US federal campaign money is much older than the electorate. In the 2020 cycle, the median contribution dollar comes from a 66-year-old, the median donor is 59, and only 9% of dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger. For comparison, the median general-election voter is 52, the median primary voter is 59 and the median non-voter is 39. Within districts, each year of candidate age adds about 0.21 years to average donor age (N = 6,098 candidate-cycles, 2012-2020). Within donors, using two-way fixed effects on 2020 donor-candidate pairs, a larger age gap lowers the chance of giving. The authors put a 30-year gap at about a 50% lower donating rate. The coefficient is -0.00328 for Democrats and -0.00317 for Republicans on a x100 scale. Pre-2020 Republican estimates are unstable because of WinRed coverage. Seed money, defined as the first 50 donations, is older and larger for older non-incumbent House candidates (N = 931). A voucher reweighting, which is a counterfactual and not an estimate, would raise funds for candidates under 66. The paper is descriptive and states that it identifies no causal effect of wealth or of policy.

For Paul's systems, its main use is as a measurement warning, not as an engine parameter. Terrier's Sphere and Participation standings run on vendor fields for political giving and turnout. The paper shows both are steeply age-graded. Terrier stratifies standings by registration but not by age, so its top deciles will lean older. Mentat's identity ladder and conduit handling line up with the paper's own data hazards: linkage built to avoid false positives, and small-donor itemization that is only complete from 2020. The paper does not bear on the Moneyball ranking, the cascade engine or the SNA layers.

bearings.paper_claim: Political contribution dollars are concentrated among older people. The median dollar comes from a 66-year-old and the mean dollar from a 64-year-old. Only 9% of dollars come from donors aged 40 or younger. Donors who reach the $2,900 limit average 63 years old. Representational weight for cohorts aged 70-80 is 200-300x that of 18-year-olds. All figures are for the 2020 cycle and US federal itemized individual contributions (DIME-linked, about 17M donors).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p. 1; Sec. 4.1 pp. 5-6 (Fig. 3, Fig. 4); Sec. 6 p. 11
bearings.system_side: Sphere = 0.45 Giving + 0.45 Volunteer + 0.10 Household. Inside Giving, the vendor high-political-contribution flag sci_ct_dnr_contribamt_high carries 1/2 of the weight, and charitable and cpi_donor carry 1/4 each. Standings are midrank percentiles, and a within-registration standing is stored. There is no within-age standing and no age control.

bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's age gradient is for federal itemized contributions in 2020. Terrier's field is a vendor's modelled flag for high political contribution amount in a district voter file (CO, OR-05, CT-01). The direction should carry over because both index political-donor wealth. The size will differ by vendor model and by district age structure. The paper says nothing about whether donors contact members more. Its access link rests on the cited Kalla and Broockman experiment, which is about announced donor status, not about individual donors' outreach.

bearings.paper_claim: Participation is age-graded at every stage. The median non-voter is 39, the median voter 52, and the median primary voter and median donor are both 59. The authors call these gaps larger than the gap between candidates and donors. Figures are for 2020, from the L2 national file of about 208M registrants.
bearings.system_side: Overall = 0.40 CUA + 0.35 Participation + 0.25 Sphere, a weighted mean of midrank standings. Participation comes from vendor turnout and engagement propensities. Sphere carries political giving. Two of the three components, 60% of nominal weight, are therefore age-loaded by construction. The only stored stratified view is by registration group.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Federal-level age medians from L2 transfer directionally to any US voter file. The size within OR-05 or CT-01 is unknown until it is measured on Terrier's own file. This bearing is a confound warning, not evidence that age-tilted standings are wrong for advocacy. Paul's ruling is that volunteers and givers are the people who engage members.

bearings.paper_claim: DIME-to-L2 donor linkage is deliberately tuned to limit false positives. It links 75% of 2012-2020 donors, and validation against Vote Smart birth years gives r = 0.95. Misses come from address changes, unregistered donors and name changes. Unlinked donors have slightly more conservative CFscores and larger average gifts, so linkage misses are not random with respect to amount.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.2 pp. 4-5; fn. 11; App. Table A4 (not extracted)
bearings.system_side: A rule ladder with no name-frequency weighting. Exact name and same zip gives AUTO. Exact name and same city, or nickname and same zip, gives HIGH. Weaker combinations go to REVIEW, and the rest are DISCARD (below_identity_threshold). Only AUTO and HIGH are kept automatically.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Both pipelines prefer precision to recall, so this supports Mentat's fail-closed posture. The paper's caveat carries over: precision-first linkage under-recovers movers and high-dollar donors. In Mentat that would bias company-attributed employee totals downward, not just add noise. The paper links donors to a voter file. Mentat links contributor rows to each other within a company roster, so the 75% figure is not a benchmark for Mentat's recall.

bearings.paper_claim: Small-donor coverage is near-complete only from 2020, because ActBlue and WinRed conduit itemization covers sub-$200 gifts. Earlier cycles miss most Republican small donors. The authors' pre-2020 Republican age-gap coefficients have the wrong sign, and they attribute that to this coverage hole.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3 p. 4; fn. 3 pp. 2-3; Sec. 5.3 p. 9
bearings.system_side: Conduit legs are kept and counted to their named recipients. Only same-recipient memo redisclosures with an eligible counterpart are removed. Employee candidate giving feeds the employee_candidate share basis in the giving forecast.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies to any Mentat cross-cycle comparison of employee (individual) giving or its partisan share that spans 2018 to 2020. The 2020 jump in itemized Republican small-dollar conduit rows is a reporting artifact, not a behavioural change. It does not affect PAC-to-candidate measures, which are committee transfers, or the current anchor cycle (2024), which falls after the break.

gaps_exposed: Terrier has no age-stratified or age-residualized standing for Sphere, Participation or Overall. Only a within-registration standing exists, at engine.py:564-571. The paper shows political giving and turnout are steeply age-graded, so top-decile lists will concentrate older residents for reasons unrelated to CU alignment. Adding an age-stratified display beside the registration one would expose this. Any such change is Paul's call.

No Mentat surface reports a coverage break for employee or individual itemized giving before and after the start of WinRed (2019-2020). Any multi-cycle employee-giving or partisan-share series that crosses 2020 could show a reporting jump that reads as behaviour.

Electoral plays (fec/engine/build_electoral_plays.py:30-33) score a contest-primary route only from same-party stance gaps. They have no term for challenger viability. The paper shows viability depends on early seed money, which depends on candidate age and personal networks (N = 931, 2020, non-incumbent House candidates only). This is a possible extension, not a defect, and the evidence is descriptive.

Mentat's identity ladder records no recall estimate. The paper's linkage shows that precision-first matching drops larger-gift donors disproportionately, so dollar totals carry an unmeasured downward bias. A hand-labelled recall sample would size it.
flags: Citation mismatch: Paul's bibliography gives DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4892936, which is the SSRN preprint. The published article's DOI, printed in the PDF, is 10.1016/j.jpubeco.2025.105451. Cite the journal DOI.

The component map lists Bonica & Grumbach 2025 under melange-influence-engine.electoral-plays. This paper says nothing about donors targeting competitive races; that finding is Bonica 2013. Do not cite it as support for electoral plays or for the competitiveness multiplier (D-104..D-108; reciprocity is NOT validated).

Pooled-coefficient rule: quote the age-gap effect by party and for 2020 only. The coefficients are D -0.00328 and R -0.00317 on the extensive margin, x100 scale, in 2020 donor-candidate pairs. Pre-2020 Republican coefficients change sign, and the generation interactions differ by stratum (Silent -0.00502 D; Gen Z positive on the intensive margin). Any cross-cycle or cross-generation pooled figure must be labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

The '30-year gap means about 50% lower donating' figure is the authors' own calculation from a two-way fixed-effects linear probability model. It is descriptive and within-donor, not causal (pp. 1-2, Sec. 7). Do not restate it as a causal or access-probability effect (D-025 spirit).

Every figure from this paper should carry its window and denominator. Donor-age medians are 2020 federal itemized individual contributions only, excluding PAC, party and presidential money (Fig. 5). Representational weights are per capita relative to 18-year-olds.
Appendix-only claims are unverified here. These include donor ideology by age (A6), wealth shares (A7) and panel robustness (A4-A6).
No rejected SNA proposal is argued here, and LDA is not used. No D-021 or SNA-rejection conflict.
This mapping is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Neither annotated-bibliography file has Paul-authored takeaways for this paper. Both are bare citation lists, and none of his 63 highlights has a note. His highlights stress the older, wealthier donor base, the seed-money and network selectorate, and the claim that age proximity drives giving. They are consistent with the component map's summary that donors are old and wealthy, which is attached to Terrier's Sphere. On Sphere, the evidence agrees with Paul's reading. It adds a consequence his notes do not draw: a giving-heavy Sphere, combined with Participation, will rank older residents higher. His Sphere ruling (45/45/10, 'leaning') rests on volunteers engaging members, and this paper neither supports nor tests that. The map's link from this paper to electoral plays and competitive-race targeting is stale or misattributed. That finding is Bonica 2013. Nothing in this paper bears on the Moneyball engine as built.

related.why: Both use the DIME contribution database and CFscores. This paper's donor-ideology-by-age claims rest on the 2013 scaling.
This paper cites Kalla and Broockman's field experiment as its causal link from donor status to access, which is the mechanism behind 'older donors shape representation'.
The within-donor design is a two-way fixed-effects regression. Imai and Kim's caution about 2FE as causal applies to reading the age-gap coefficients.
Both face individual-donor identity resolution in FEC data without unique IDs. Kim et al. use constrained graph clustering, and Bonica-Grumbach use precision-first voter-file linkage.
Bonica-Grumbach study individual hard money only and exclude PACs. Furnas et al. separate PAC from lobbying money. Together they mark which money stream each claim covers.
